targets.name: shared/spread/three-windows
targets.why: The ordinary multi-window loader: every window is a target and the budget is the window count, so one demand of N puts exactly N carriers out and never 2N.

targets.name: shared/spread/the-operator-arrangement-decides
targets.why: Windows come back in the order the OPERATOR dragged them, not in name order. The admin screen offers a reorder handle, Core persists the arrangement and syncs it down, and it used to be discarded on arrival — no ordinal on the wire, no ordinal column in the Edge cache, and a cache read that re-sorted by name. The intent was accepted, stored, transmitted and ignored. Since the funnel case takes the first window and spreading fills in order, this decides which window a carrier physically goes to.

targets.name: shared/spread/ten-windows-do-not-reorder-themselves
targets.why: The trap the fallback exists to avoid. Plants name windows W1, W2, W3 and plain text order matches intent exactly — until a loader reaches ten, where plain text puts W10 before W2 and the funnel target silently moves. Here the operator's arrangement already answers it; the companion case below is the same names with nothing arranged, which is what the number-aware fallback has to get right on its own.

targets.name: shared/spread/no-arrangement-falls-back-to-natural-name-order
targets.why: Nothing dragged, so every ordinal is zero — which is also exactly what a Core that predates the ordinal field sends. Every comparison ties and the order comes from the names, number-aware: W2 before W10. This is the mixed-version case and the never-touched-loader case at once, and it is the one that has to keep working unchanged at plants that have never used the reorder handle.

targets.name: shared/funnel/first-window-only
targets.why: A loader configured to take one window at a time delivers to its first window on a budget of 1 — a real node, never the loader's own identity token, which is not a node.

targets.name: shared/funnel/first-is-the-one-the-operator-put-first
targets.why: Which window the funnel picks follows the same order. Paired with the spread case so the two facts cannot be fixed apart: the funnel target is just the head of the list the spread case pins.

targets.name: shared/single-window/spread-degrades-to-one
targets.why: A one-window shared loader answers the same whether it spreads or funnels, so turning the setting on only changes loaders that actually have several windows.

targets.name: shared/payload-not-in-set
targets.why: A payload the loader does not carry has no target here. Nil and budget zero is a normal 'not this loader' answer, not a failure — the caller must not treat it as one.

targets.name: shared/blank-payload-is-agnostic
targets.why: A blank payload is the payload-agnostic transitional case and still resolves. It is NOT the same as an unknown payload, which resolves to nothing.

targets.name: shared/member-named-is-ignored
targets.why: Naming a member window changes nothing for a shared loader: the windows share one budget and the free-window assignment picks the slot. Only dedicated layouts honour the member.

targets.name: shared/buffer-slot-counts-as-a-window
targets.why: home_kind separates a payload-pinned home from a kept-partial buffer, but nothing filters buffers out of a shared loader's windows on either side — so a buffer slot is a delivery target and a unit of budget. Pinned as-is because both sides agree today; the filter, if wanted, belongs where both would inherit it.

targets.name: shared/no-windows-configured
targets.why: A shared loader created in the admin screen with no members dragged in yet has nowhere to deliver and must fail closed rather than resolve to its own identity.
targets.core_only: the Edge constructor refuses to build a shared loader with zero windows, so this shape cannot exist there to be asked

targets.name: dedicated/first-match-no-member
targets.why: With no member named, the payload picks its position by first match. Budget 1: dedicated positions are independent one-bin slots and never share a budget.

targets.name: dedicated/member-wins-over-first-match
targets.why: The same payload loaded at two positions: the carrier goes to the position the signal named, not to whichever sorts first. Without this, a low reading at one position restocks the other.

targets.name: dedicated/member-not-serving-payload-falls-back
targets.why: A member that names a position which does not carry the payload is not honoured — it falls back to first match rather than delivering the wrong part to the named node.

targets.name: dedicated/member-with-blank-payload
targets.why: A payload-agnostic ask that names a member goes to that member whatever it carries. This is the transitional shape, and it must not fall through to first match.

targets.name: dedicated/unassigned-position-matches-blank-payload
targets.why: A position dragged in but not yet assigned a payload carries the empty string, so a payload-agnostic first-match lands on it. Pinned because it is surprising: the shape exists between an operator dropping a tile and choosing its part.

targets.name: dedicated/payload-not-served
targets.why: No position carries the payload, so there is no target. Same normal 'not this loader' answer as the shared case.

targets.name: dedicated/funnel-setting-is-inert
targets.why: The window setting means nothing to a dedicated loader — its positions never shared a budget — so the answer is identical with it on. A future change that lets it leak into dedicated routing fails here.

sizing.name: exact-multiple
sizing.why: A gap that divides evenly into carrier capacity asks for exactly that many.

sizing.name: rounds-up
sizing.why: A partial carrier's worth of shortfall still needs a whole carrier. Rounding down would leave the loop permanently short of its threshold.

sizing.name: one-unit-short
sizing.why: The smallest real gap still asks for one carrier — the boundary rounding-down would get wrong.

sizing.name: at-threshold
sizing.why: Exactly at threshold is not below it. Nothing is wanted, and that is a normal answer rather than a failure.

sizing.name: above-threshold
sizing.why: Above threshold likewise asks for nothing.

sizing.name: negative-current-sizes-from-zero
sizing.why: Springfield reported -443. Sized from that reading the gap was 455 and the answer 26 carriers — every number computed from a count already known to be broken. The gap is sized from 0 instead. Ordering still CONTINUES: a negative total means material left the books, which is when the loop needs stock. A broken count does not get to size the order and does not get to cancel it.

sizing.name: negative-current-small
sizing.why: The clamp is to zero, not an offset: a small negative reading gives the same answer as an empty loop.

sizing.name: no-per-bin-capacity
sizing.why: A payload with no catalog capacity makes 'how many carriers' unanswerable. It is a configuration error, and the answer is to create nothing and say so — never to fall back to counting bins, which is the fixed floor that made loaders over-order.

sizing.name: negative-per-bin-capacity
sizing.why: Same answer for a negative capacity. The guard is <= 0, not == 0, so a garbage catalog row cannot produce a negative or wildly large carrier count.

sizing.name: capacity-one
sizing.why: One unit per carrier means one carrier per unit of gap. The degenerate case, pinned because it is where an off-by-one in the rounding shows up largest.

sizing.name: huge-gap-single-carrier-capacity
sizing.why: Sizing does not bound itself. It returns what the loop needs; what actually gets created is bounded later by free windows and what is already inbound. A caller that treats this number as the count to create is the over-ordering failure again.

sizing.name: zero-threshold
sizing.why: A loader with no threshold configured is never below it.
